intro.title: Looking at a data frame
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real data comes as a table: one **row** per thing (a trip, an order, a student) and one **column** per fact about it. In R, a table is a **data frame**. Each column is a vector, so everything from the last quests works on it.

This quest uses trips from Riverside Bikes. Each challenge starts with the code that makes the data frame:

```
trips <- data.frame(
  id = 1:8,
  station = c("Park", "River", "Park", "Market", "River", "Park", "Market", "River"),
  minutes = c(12, 47, 30, 8, 55, 15, 22, 35),
  km = c(2.4, 9.4, 5.1, 1.2, 10.3, 2.9, 3.8, 6.0),
  member = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
```

The first thing to do with any data is look at it. Type the name to see the whole table, or use these for a quick look:

| Function | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `head(trips)` | the first 6 rows (`head(trips, 3)` for 3) |
| `tail(trips)` | the last 6 rows |
| `nrow(trips)`, `ncol(trips)` | the number of rows and columns |
| `dim(trips)` | both: rows, then columns |
| `names(trips)` | the column names |
| `str(trips)` | every column with its type and first values |

`str()` is the most useful of all: it shows at a glance whether each column has the type you expect. `num` is numeric, `int` integer, `chr` text and `logi` TRUE/FALSE. A column of numbers that comes up as `chr` needs fixing before you can calculate with it.

intro.title: Making a data frame
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most data frames are read from a file, which comes in a later quest. For small tables, and for trying things out, you make one with `data.frame()`. Give each column a name and a vector:

```
menu <- data.frame(
  item  = c("latte", "tea", "cake"),
  price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2),
  vegan = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
menu
```

Every column must have the same length, because each row needs a value in every column. If the lengths differ, R gives an error such as "arguments imply differing number of rows". The one exception is a single value, which R repeats down the column: `data.frame(item = c("tea", "cake"), shop = "Corner Café")`.

You can also build a data frame from vectors you already have: `data.frame(day = days, steps = steps)` puts two matching vectors side by side, which is exactly what they have been all along.

Text columns stay as text. (Very old R turned them into factors automatically; since R 4.0 it doesn't.) Make a factor yourself when you want one: `size = factor(c("S", "M"), levels = c("S", "M", "L"))`.

intro.title: Columns with $
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A data frame is a set of named columns, and `$` gets one out by name. This stage uses the Riverside Bikes trips again:

```
trips <- data.frame(
  id = 1:8,
  station = c("Park", "River", "Park", "Market", "River", "Park", "Market", "River"),
  minutes = c(12, 47, 30, 8, 55, 15, 22, 35),
  km = c(2.4, 9.4, 5.1, 1.2, 10.3, 2.9, 3.8, 6.0),
  member = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
```

What you get with `$` is an ordinary vector, so everything from the Vectors quest works on it:

```
trips$minutes                # 12 47 30 8 55 15 22 35
mean(trips$minutes)          # 28
sum(trips$member)            # 5 members
trips$station[trips$minutes > 40]
```

`trips[["minutes"]]` does the same as `trips$minutes`. It is handy when the column name is in a variable: `col <- "km"; trips[[col]]`.

**Making a new column** works the same way: assign to a name that doesn't exist yet. Because columns are vectors, a calculation on one column gives a value for every row:

```
trips$cost <- 1 + 0.15 * trips$minutes
trips$speed <- round(trips$km / (trips$minutes / 60), 1)
trips$long <- trips$minutes > 30
```

Assigning to an existing column replaces it, for example to fix its type: `trips$station <- factor(trips$station)`. To remove a column, assign `NULL` to it: `trips$long <- NULL`.

`ifelse()` is great for new columns: `trips$fare <- ifelse(trips$member, 0, trips$cost)` makes the ride free for members.

intro.title: Rows and columns with [ , ]
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Square brackets on a data frame take **two** parts, separated by a comma: which rows, then which columns. `df[rows, columns]`. Leave a part empty to mean "all of them".

This stage uses orders from Corner Café:

```
orders <- data.frame(
  order = 101:110,
  day = c("Mon", "Mon", "Tue", "Tue", "Tue", "Wed", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Fri"),
  drink = c("latte", "tea", "mocha", "latte", "latte", "tea", "chai", "latte", "mocha", "tea"),
  size = c("M", "S", "L", "M", "S", "M", "L", "L", "M", "S"),
  price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.4, 2.9, 2.5, 3.8, 3.9, 4.2, 2.2)
)
```

Rows and columns can be picked by position, by name, or (for rows) by a condition:

```
orders[1, ]                          # the first row, every column
orders[, "price"]                    # every row, the price column (a vector)
orders[1:3, c("drink", "price")]     # first 3 rows, two columns
orders[orders$price > 4, ]           # rows where the price is over 4
```

Don't forget the comma! `orders[1, ]` is the first row, but `orders[1]` (no comma) is the first **column**, as a one-column data frame.

A single value is `orders[2, "drink"]`: row 2, column `drink`. You can assign to any of these to change values: `orders[2, "price"] <- 2.7`.

Picking one column gives a vector; picking several gives a smaller data frame. That's usually what you want, and it's good to know when a function complains that it expected one or the other.

questions.prompt: Why does `df[df$x > 5, ]` need the comma?

choices.label: Before the comma picks rows and after it columns; without it R picks columns

questions.explanation: With nothing after the comma, every column is kept.

questions.prompt: What does `df[, "x"]` give?

choices.label: The column x, as a vector

questions.explanation: An empty rows part means every row.

choices.label: `df[1, ]` is the first row; `df[1]` is the first column

questions.explanation: Without a comma, the brackets pick columns.

intro.title: Filtering rows
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Keeping only the rows you care about is called **filtering**. This stage uses the Riverside Bikes trips:

```
trips <- data.frame(
  id = 1:8,
  station = c("Park", "River", "Park", "Market", "River", "Park", "Market", "River"),
  minutes = c(12, 47, 30, 8, 55, 15, 22, 35),
  km = c(2.4, 9.4, 5.1, 1.2, 10.3, 2.9, 3.8, 6.0),
  member = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
```

You already know how: put a condition in the rows part of the brackets. Every tool for conditions works, because each column is a vector:

```
trips[trips$minutes > 30, ]                              # long trips
trips[trips$station == "Park" & trips$member, ]          # members from Park
trips[trips$station %in% c("Park", "River"), ]           # two stations
trips[!trips$member, ]                                   # non-members
```

Writing `trips$` again and again gets long. `subset()` does the same with the column names alone, and can pick columns too:

```
subset(trips, minutes > 30)
subset(trips, station == "Park" & member, select = c(id, minutes))
```

A filtered table is a data frame like any other, so you can count its rows or summarise a column of it: `nrow(subset(trips, member))` is the number of member trips, and `mean(subset(trips, member)$minutes)` their average length.

One trap: if a column has `NA`s, a condition gives `NA` for those rows, and `trips[cond, ]` adds a row of NAs to the result. `subset()` leaves those rows out, which is one more reason to prefer it. (`which(cond)` works too.)

intro.title: Sorting rows
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This stage sorts the Corner Café orders:

```
orders <- data.frame(
  order = 101:110,
  day = c("Mon", "Mon", "Tue", "Tue", "Tue", "Wed", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Fri"),
  drink = c("latte", "tea", "mocha", "latte", "latte", "tea", "chai", "latte", "mocha", "tea"),
  size = c("M", "S", "L", "M", "S", "M", "L", "L", "M", "S"),
  price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.4, 2.9, 2.5, 3.8, 3.9, 4.2, 2.2)
)
```

Remember `order()` from the Vectors quest? It gives the positions in sorted order, and that is exactly what goes in the rows part of the brackets to sort a whole table by one column:

```
orders[order(orders$price), ]                       # cheapest first
orders[order(orders$price, decreasing = TRUE), ]    # dearest first
```

Every row moves as a whole, so the drink, day and price of an order stay together. (Using `sort()` on a column would only sort that column.)

To break ties, give `order()` a second column: `orders[order(orders$day, orders$price), ]` sorts by day, and by price within each day. For "largest first" on a number column mixed with other columns, put a minus in front of it: `order(orders$day, -orders$price)`.

Text sorts alphabetically, so weekdays sorted as text come out Fri, Mon, Thu, Tue, Wed. Make the column a factor with the levels in order, and `order()` follows the levels instead.

Sorting and `head()` together give a top few: `head(orders[order(-orders$price), ], 3)` is the three dearest orders.

questions.prompt: Why use `order()` and not `sort()` to sort a data frame?

choices.label: `order()` gives positions, so whole rows move together

questions.explanation: `sort()` gives sorted values of one column only.

questions.prompt: What does `order(c(2, 1, 2), c(9, 8, 7))` give?
questions.explanation: The 1 comes first (position 2). The two 2s tie, so the second vector breaks the tie: 7 (position 3) before 9 (position 1).

questions.prompt: Why does a minus, as in `order(-df$price)`, sort from largest to smallest?

questions.explanation: Text sorts alphabetically, not in week order.

intro.title: Summaries and missing values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This stage uses the Elm Street garden's harvest. One weight was never written down:

```
harvest <- data.frame(
  plot = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C", "D", "D"),
  crop = c("tomatoes", "beans", "tomatoes", "kale", "beans", "kale", "tomatoes", "beans"),
  kg = c(12.4, 3.6, 9.8, NA, 4.1, 2.7, 14.2, 2.9),
  family = c("Silva", "Silva", "Okafor", "Okafor", "Li", "Li", "Mensah", "Mensah")
)
```

`summary()` gives a quick overview of every column at once. For number columns it shows the minimum, quartiles, median, mean and maximum, and how many `NA`s there are. It is the fastest way to spot odd values and gaps:

```
summary(harvest)
summary(harvest$kg)
```

To find the gaps, `is.na()` works on a column, and `colSums(is.na(harvest))` counts the NAs in every column at once. To see the incomplete rows themselves, use `complete.cases()`, which is TRUE for rows with no NA anywhere:

```
harvest[!complete.cases(harvest), ]   # the rows with a gap
na.omit(harvest)                      # every row without a gap
```

Be careful with `na.omit()`: it drops a whole row even when only one column is missing. Often it is better to leave the row and use `na.rm = TRUE` in the summary you need: `sum(harvest$kg, na.rm = TRUE)`.

For several number columns at once, `colMeans()` and `colSums()` average or add up every column of a table of numbers, also with `na.rm = TRUE`.

intro.title: Combining tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Data often comes in more than one table. Two ways to put tables together:

**Stacking** adds the rows of one table below another. Both need the same column names. `rbind()` does it ("row bind"):

```
monday  <- data.frame(item = c("latte", "tea"), qty = c(2, 1))
tuesday <- data.frame(item = c("cake", "latte"), qty = c(3, 1))
rbind(monday, tuesday)   # 4 rows
```

**Merging** matches rows on a shared column, the **key**. Say one table has what was sold and another the menu prices. `merge()` looks up each sale's item in the menu and adds the price:

```
sales <- data.frame(item = c("latte", "tea", "cake", "latte", "scone"), qty = c(2, 1, 3, 1, 2))
menu  <- data.frame(item = c("latte", "tea", "cake", "chai"), price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.8))
merge(sales, menu, by = "item")
```

By default `merge()` keeps only rows that match in **both** tables: the scone (not on the menu) and the chai (never sold) are dropped, and the result is sorted by the key. Add `all.x = TRUE` to keep every row of the first table, with `NA` where nothing matched. That's how you find sales of items missing from the menu.

To add a whole new column from a vector of the same length, `cbind()` ("column bind") or plain `df$new <- …` both work.

per_family <- tapply(all_rows$kg, all_rows$family, sum)
per_crop <- tapply(all_rows$kg, all_rows$crop, sum)
cat("Families:", length(per_family), "\n")
cat("Total:", sum(all_rows$kg), "kg\n")
cat("Top family:", names(which.max(per_family)), paste0("(", max(per_family), " kg)"), "\n")
cat("Top crop:", names(which.max(per_crop)), "\n")", c(), output = TRUE)
